abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel computational model that fundamentally reconceptualizes the relationship between classical and quantum computational paradigms. While existing quantum complexity classes such as BQP have been defined primarily through oracle separations, we propose the concept of resource-adaptive quantum computation, where the complexity classification depends not only on problem instance size but also on quantum coherence characteristics. Our approach establishes a hierarchical framework that captures the continuum between purely classical and fully quantum computational power, revealing previously unrecognized intermediate complexity classes. We demonstrate that certain problems believed to be outside BQP can be efficiently solved under this new model when quantum coherence is appropriately managed. The technical contribution includes new complete problems for these intermediate classes and establish tight relationships between coherence requirements and computational hardness. This work opens several research directions in computational complexity theory, particularly concerning the structural properties of quantum advantage and the role of decoherence in determining computational boundaries. Our findings suggest that the traditional discrete classification of computational complexity may need to be replaced by more nuanced models that account for continuous quantum properties.

We present improved upper and lower bounds for the computational complexity of computing the permanent of n×n matrices over the Boolean semiring. The permanent function has been a central object of study in combinatorial optimization and computational complexity, with significant implications for counting versions of NP-complete problems. While previous work established that permanent computation requires time super-polynomial in n under certain complexity-theoretic assumptions, we sharpen these bounds substantially. Our main technical contribution involves a refined analysis of algebraic branching programs combined with a new combinatorial decomposition technique that exploits structural properties of matrix minors. We prove that computing the permanent of dense matrices requires time Ω(n^{ω+o(1)}) where ω is the exponent of matrix multiplication, improving upon the previous Ω(n^{ω-0.5}) lower bound. Additionally, we show that any algorithm computing permanent using algebraic methods must exhibit exponential behavior on certain structured matrix families. These results strengthen the evidence that permanent computation is intractable and provide new insights into the complexity landscape of algebraic computation.

This paper presents τ-Calculus, a foundational programming language theory framework that uniformly integrates quantitative reasoning about time, resource consumption, and program behavior within a single semantic theory. Traditional approaches to programming language theory treat these concerns as orthogonal, requiring separate formalisms for operational semantics, denotational semantics, and program analysis. Our system introduces a novel semantic framework where quantitative aspects emerge naturally from the same underlying mathematical structure, eliminating the need for ad-hoc extensions. The core innovation lies in our generalized algebraic structure that subsumes both classical domain theory and weighted automata theory as special cases. We demonstrate the expressiveness of τ-Calculus through case studies in real-time systems, probabilistic programming, and energy-aware computing, showing how a single semantic framework can uniformly reason about diverse quantitative properties. The paper also develops a type system and associated program logic that enable compositional verification of quantitative program properties. This work provides theoretical foundations for next-generation programming languages that treat quantitative concerns as first-class citizens.

We design and analyze a new family of consensus protocols for asynchronous distributed systems that achieve optimal Byzantine fault tolerance with significantly improved communication complexity. Consensus in distributed computing remains fundamental to fault-tolerant systems, yet existing Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols incur substantial communication overhead that limits their practical applicability. Our proposed protocol, called LightChain, reduces the message complexity from O(n^2) to O(n log n) while maintaining the standard n > 3f threshold for Byzantine resilience where f represents the number of faulty nodes. The key innovation involves a novel authenticated data structure that enables efficient verification of consensus messages without requiring all-to-all communication. We provide a rigorous formal verification of LightChain using refinement mappings and establish its safety and liveness properties under standard asynchronous network assumptions. Performance evaluations demonstrate that our protocol achieves 40% reduction in communication overhead compared to state-of-the-art solutions while maintaining comparable latency characteristics. This work significantly advances practical Byzantine fault tolerance for distributed ledgers and blockchain systems.
